The silt-glass of dusk on Virellia is the color of bruised copper, and that is when the kharren comes out.

It is not large by the standards of its world—about the length of a human arm if you count the trailing veil—but it occupies space strangely, as if the air has agreed to be thicker around it. The body is a soft, low dome of translucent cartilage, the color of wet slate with a faint green oil-sheen where the light hits. Through that skin you can see the slow pulse of three inner sacs, each the size of a grape, drifting in a fluid that never quite settles. They are not organs in any tidy sense. They are clocks. When one drifts left, the creature turns. When two align, it feeds. When all three stack, it stops, and the ground beneath it goes quiet.

It has no legs. Instead, a fringe of hollow cilia—thousands of them, glassy and jointless—rolls in coordinated waves. They do not push so much as they *invite* the silt to move, and the body follows. Leave a trail and it looks like a sentence written in a language that prefers curves. The cilia taste as they walk. Salt, metal, the faint sweetness of buried lichen, the iron-tang of a rival's passage: all of it is read in the same motion as locomotion. A kharren that has crossed your path knows what you had for breakfast three days ago, if breakfast left minerals in your sweat.

At the front, where a face would be if faces were obligatory, there is a single horizontal slit that never fully closes. It is not a mouth. It is a lamp. Inside, a colony of symbiotic microbes burns a cold blue-white, fed on sulfur the kharren siphons from the crust through a needle-fine siphon it can extend and retract like a thought. The light is not for seeing. Kharren are nearly blind in any human sense. The lamp is a signal and a weapon of manners: dim it, and nearby kharren treat you as kin; flare it to a hard white, and the silt-mites that infest the feeding grounds flee in a living sheet. The creature farms those mites the way a shepherd farms panic—never killing the flock, only moving it onto richer ground, then grazing the film they leave behind.

Its true sense is pressure. Along the dome run six shallow grooves, each lined with a membrane thinner than a soap bubble. These read the footfalls of things a kilometer off, the flex of the ice-plates under the southern sea, even the minute sag of the atmosphere when one of Virellia's twin moons pulls close. A kharren standing still is not resting. It is listening to the planet breathe, and adjusting its three inner clocks to match.

It reproduces without meeting another of its kind. Once every long winter, when the copper dusk lasts for weeks and the lichen goes dormant, a kharren splits a bead of its own fluid into the silt and walks away. The bead does not hatch. It *remembers*. Over months it accretes mineral, cilia, and a borrowed scrap of microbial light, and when it finally rises it already knows the local footfall-map, the best mite-grounds, the taste of every trail its parent ever crossed. Inheritance, on Virellia, is a sediment.

They are not social, exactly, but they are not alone. At the edge of the feeding grounds you sometimes see three or four domes halted in a loose arc, lamps turned down to the same dim blue, grooves aligned toward the same distant flex in the ice. They are not speaking. They are agreeing, for a little while, about what the world is doing—and then, without a signal you could name, they roll apart, each writing its own curved sentence back into the silt.

CREATURE DESCRIPTION:
The glassback is a slow, translucent grazer that lives in the twilight forests of a tidally locked world, where one hemisphere never sees the sun and the other never loses it. It stays in the narrow band between those extremes, where the light is dim and the air is always cold and wet.

It is about the size of a horse but shaped more like a low, segmented raft. Six jointed legs, jointed in the wrong places by terrestrial standards, hold its body only a hand’s width above the moss. The legs are pale and hollow-looking, with dark rings of muscle at each bend, and they move in a rolling wave so the animal never fully stops. Its underside is soft and pale, lined with rows of fine, hairlike filaments that taste the ground as it walks, sampling salts, fungal sugars, and the faint chemical traces of other glassbacks.

The back is the striking part. A broad, slightly arched carapace of living crystal covers it from neck to tail, thin enough that you can see organs shifting underneath like lanterns in fog. The plates are not true mineral; they are a protein lattice the creature grows and continually sheds, clear when the animal is calm and milky when it is stressed. Symbiotic algae live in thin channels inside the glass, feeding on the weak light and leaking sugars into the creature’s blood. In return, the glassback’s slow warmth and mineral-rich waste keep the algae alive in a place that would otherwise starve them. At dusk—such as dusk is, on that world—the algae fluoresce, and a glassback moving through the forest looks like a drifting pane of green-blue light.

Its head is small and wedge-shaped, with no eyes. Instead, a fan of pressure-sensitive pits runs along both sides of the skull, reading air currents and the minute vibrations of fungal fruiting bodies under the moss. A single slit mouth opens along the underside of the wedge. Inside are not teeth but concentric rings of rasping pads, which it presses into the soft crust of the forest floor to scrape up bacterial films and the sweet, rotting caps of the low fungi it prefers.

Glassbacks do not vocalize in air. They talk by changing the tension of the crystal plates, which ring at frequencies too low for a human ear but strong enough to shiver the moss for meters around. A herd crossing a ridge sounds, to instruments, like distant ice cracking. They gather in loose groups of a dozen or so, keeping just close enough that their vibrations overlap, and they will stop and stand still for hours if a storm wind drowns the signal.

They have one clear predator: a low, armored burrower that hunts by heat. A glassback’s defense is not speed. When threatened, it dumps stored fluid into the channels of its carapace, clouding the crystal and bleeding heat so quickly that its thermal outline collapses into the cold ground. It then lowers itself until the legs fold flat and remains motionless, indistinguishable from a slab of wet ice, until the burrower passes. If it is caught anyway, the plates shatter outward in a spray of sharp, living shards, and the animal beneath is soft, slow, and almost certainly finished.

Young glassbacks are born already glassed, small and nearly invisible, and spend their first season clinging beneath an adult’s belly, feeding on algal sugars that seep through the parent’s skin. They leave only when their own plates grow thick enough to hold light.

Seen from a distance, in that permanent half-light, a herd of them looks less like animals than like pieces of the sky that have learned to walk.

They do not have eyes. A ring of photosensitive cells sits under a thin membrane on the upper surface, sensing only the gradient between glare and night. They orient by that gradient the way a plant orients by light, always drifting so that the brighter side of the world stays just outside their comfort.
